name: checksec
one_line: check the security protections of a binary
plain: `checksec` reads a program file and tells you which defences were compiled in: stack canaries, non-executable stack (NX), position-independent code (PIE), RELRO and more. In a pwn challenge this tells you which attacks are possible before you write any exploit.
The check exists as a shell script (`checksec --file=BINARY`) and as a pwntools command (`pwn checksec BINARY`); the meanings are the same.
when: First step on any binary-exploitation challenge.
Decide between shellcode on the stack, ROP, ret2libc or GOT overwrite.
Check whether a kernel or running process has hardening on.
Audit what a build system produced.

examples.title: Check a binary
examples.explain: Prints RELRO, Stack, NX, PIE, RPATH, RUNPATH, Symbols and FORTIFY, with colours for good and bad.

examples.explain: Gives a shorter report and also the architecture and whether the binary is stripped.

examples.title: Check a whole folder
examples.explain: Reports every binary in the folder.

examples.title: Check a running process
examples.explain: Shows the protections in effect for that process.

examples.title: Check the kernel
examples.explain: Lists kernel hardening options if the configuration is readable.

examples.title: Machine-readable output
examples.explain: Formats: cli, csv, xml, json. Handy for scripts.

examples.title: Reading the result
examples.cmd:
NX disabled  ->  shellcode on the stack can run
No canary found  ->  a plain stack overflow can overwrite the return address
No PIE  ->  addresses are fixed, so ROP and ret2plt are easy
examples.explain: Match each finding to the attack it allows or blocks.

options.plain: Check all files in a directory (verbose lists each).
Check a running process by name.
Check the libraries loaded by a process.
Check FORTIFY_SOURCE protections of a file.
Update the script to the newest version.
Partial: the GOT is writable (GOT overwrite possible). Full: it is read-only after start-up.
A random value placed before the return address; overflow is detected unless you leak or avoid it.
Data memory cannot run as code: shellcode on the stack fails; use ROP.
The program loads at a random address each run: you need an address leak.
Custom library paths inside the binary: possible library hijack.
Whether names remain for debugging; whether safer copies of libc functions are used.

mistakes: Reading a result as a guarantee: protections can be bypassed with leaks and ROP.
Forgetting that libc and the kernel (ASLR) add their own protections: check cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space.
Using the pwntools and shell versions and expecting identical wording.
Running checksec on a file that is not an ELF (it reports nothing).
try: Compile a C program with gcc -fno-stack-protector -z execstack -no-pie and check it.
Compile it with default options and compare.
Write down which attack each missing protection would allow.
see_also: gcc(1), gdb(1), readelf(1), objdump(1), pwntools, ROPgadget(1), file(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
